clinicalPearls: A diagnosis of exclusion: severe recurrent loin pain with macroscopic or microscopic haematuria and no identifiable urological or glomerular cause.
Pain may be unilateral or bilateral, is often severe and disproportionate to findings, and may be triggered by minor events.
Extensive imaging and cystoscopy are needed to exclude stones, obstruction, tumour and vascular anomalies.
Renal biopsy may show C3 deposition in arteriolar walls or glomerular basement membrane abnormalities, but is often near-normal and mainly serves to exclude glomerulonephritis.
There is a strong association with psychological distress and analgesic dependence, so multidisciplinary pain management is central.
Actively exclude nutcracker syndrome and thin basement membrane disease as mimics.
Invasive options such as nerve blocks, renal denervation, autotransplantation and nephrectomy are last resort with inconsistent and often disappointing results.
reference.pathophysiology: The mechanism is poorly understood and probably heterogeneous. Proposed contributors include a renal microvascular or glomerular abnormality allowing red cells to escape into tubules with tubular obstruction and capsular distension, abnormally thick or thin glomerular basement membranes, complement (C3) deposition in vessel walls, intrarenal vascular spasm, and crystalluria causing microtrauma. Altered central pain processing and visceral hypersensitivity are increasingly recognised components, and by definition no obstructing, neoplastic, infective or defined glomerular cause is found.
additionalDifferentials: Thin basement membrane disease or IgA nephropathy
Medullary sponge kidney or musculoskeletal loin pain
additionalInvestigations: Urinalysis and microscopy for dysmorphic red cells and casts
CT urography for stones, obstruction and masses
Doppler or cross-sectional venography for nutcracker phenomenon
Cystoscopy to localise bleeding and exclude bladder pathology
Glomerular screen (complement, autoimmune serology, protein quantification)
redFlags: Features suggesting malignancy such as a mass or unexplained weight loss
Signs of urinary obstruction or infection with sepsis
New proteinuria, red-cell casts or rising creatinine suggesting glomerulonephritis
reference.prognosis: It is a chronic and often debilitating condition with a relapsing course; pain diminishes over time in some patients, but many endure years of symptoms and invasive interventions frequently fail to provide durable relief.
pitfalls: Making the diagnosis without adequately excluding treatable causes such as stones, nutcracker syndrome and glomerulonephritis
Escalating opioids without a multidisciplinary pain strategy
Proceeding to nephrectomy or autotransplantation with unrealistic expectations and risk of contralateral recurrence
Dismissing the patient as functional and missing evolving organic disease
references: Oxford Handbook of Nephrology and Hypertension
